title: Pre-emption Suit (Shufa) Law in Bangladesh
metaDescription: Reclaim ancestral or co-owned land sold to an outsider via a Pre-emption (Shufa) suit under Section 96 SAT Act 1950. Learn deadlines, deposits & legal steps.
keywords: Right of Shufa Bangladesh land law
heroIntro: Under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (for agricultural land) and Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (for urban/non-agricultural land), a co-sharer by inheritance can legally buy back a co-sharer's share sold to a stranger by filing a Pre-emption (Shufa) case within 2 to 4 months and depositing the consideration money plus statutory compensation in court.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: Pre-emption (Shufa) in Bangladesh
points: Governing Laws: Section 96, State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 (agricultural); Section 24, Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (urban).
Limitation Period: 2 months (Section 96 SAT Act, post-2006 amendment) or 4 months (Section 24 NAT Act) from notice or knowledge.
Mandatory Deposit: Full deed consideration money + 25% compensation (SAT Act) or 5% compensation (NAT Act) + 8% annual interest.
Who Can Claim: Only a co-sharer tenant by inheritance (after the 2006 amendment to Section 96), not contiguous landowners.

sections.h2: What Is the Right of Pre-emption (Shufa) in Bangladesh?
sections.content:
Pre-emption (known as Haq-e-Shufa in Islamic law and Ogrokroyadhikar in Bangla) is a statutory preferential right enabling an existing co-sharer of an undivided ancestral property to step into the shoes of an outside buyer and acquire the sold share at the same price. The law exists to prevent strangers from disrupting family homesteads and fragmenting inherited holdings.

Following the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006, statutory pre-emption under Section 96 is restricted exclusively to co-sharers by inheritance—meaning co-sharers by purchase and contiguous landowners can no longer file Section 96 pre-emption cases for agricultural land. However, Muslim personal law Shufa rules may still apply in specific uncodified contexts if strict Islamic formalities (Talab-i-Mowasibat and Talab-i-Ishhad) are proved.

For NRB heirs who discover a sibling sold their joint ancestral plot without notice, pre-emption is often faster than a family property partition suit. Speak with a specialist land lawyer in Bangladesh immediately because the limitation window is extremely short.

sections.h2: Section 96 SAT Act vs Section 24 NAT Act: Key Differences
sections.content:
Choosing the wrong statute between agricultural land and non-agricultural (municipal/urban) land is the most common reason pre-emption petitions are dismissed at the threshold. The land's recorded classification and location govern which Act applies.

FeatureSection 96, SAT Act 1950 (Agricultural)Section 24, NAT Act 1949 (Non-Agricultural)
Eligible ClaimantOnly a co-sharer by inheritance (post-2006 amendment).Co-sharer tenant in non-agricultural land (e.g., municipal/urban plots).
Limitation Period2 months from service of notice or knowledge of sale.4 months from service of notice or knowledge of transfer.
Mandatory DepositConsideration price + 25% statutory compensation + 8% p.a. interest.Consideration price + 5% statutory compensation.
Exempt TransfersHeba/gift to blood relatives within 3 degrees, exchange, partition, will.Transfer to co-sharer, exchange, partition, or gift to specified relatives.

Always verify the land classification (Nal, Vita, Chala, or Danga) in the latest Khatian using our online khatian and mutation guide and check inheritance share rules before filing.

sections.h2: Statutory Deadlines and Mandatory Court Deposits
sections.content:
Under both Section 96(3) of the SAT Act, 1950 and Section 24(2) of the NAT Act, 1949, a pre-emption application is liable to outright dismissal if the petitioner fails to deposit the full consideration money stated in the sale deed plus the statutory compensation into court at the time of filing.

Under Section 96(1), the 2-month deadline runs from the date the co-sharer receives statutory notice of the transfer under Section 89, or—if no notice was served—from the date the co-sharer first gains actual knowledge of the sale. Crucially, the Supreme Court has consistently held that Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 (condonation of delay) does not extend the 2-month or 4-month statutory pre-emption period, though Section 18 (fraudulent concealment) may apply if the buyer deliberately hid the registration.

Where a buyer inflates the deed price artificially to deter co-sharers, the court can hold an inquiry under Section 96(4) to determine the actual consideration paid. Review Dhaka land purchase valuation rules for how mouza rates interact with deed prices.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Procedure to File a Pre-emption Case
sections.content:
Because pre-emption is registered as a Miscellaneous Case (Misc. Case) rather than an ordinary civil suit, speed and exact compliance with deposit rules are decisive:

  1. Obtain Certified Copy of the Sale Deed: Immediately collect the certified copy (Nakal) of the impugned Saf Kabala deed from the Sub-Registry Office to confirm the exact consideration price and registration date.
  2. Verify Co-Sharer Status & Land Classification: Gather the ancestor's CS/SA/RS/BS Khatian and Warish Certificate proving you are a co-sharer by inheritance in the same jote or holding.
  3. Deposit Consideration + Compensation via Treasury Challan: Deposit the exact deed price plus 25% compensation (under SAT Act) or 5% (under NAT Act) into the court's treasury account before or simultaneously with filing.
  4. File Pre-emption Misc. Case: Submit the verified petition before the Assistant Judge Court having territorial jurisdiction, naming both the seller co-sharer and the outside buyer as opposite parties.
  5. Attend Trial & Obtain Execution Order: Once allowed, the court transfers the buyer's title to the pre-emptor, who then updates mutation—see our land title and possession guide or consult Advocate Md. Shah Alam.

NRBs abroad can initiate this within the 2-month window using an urgent Embassy-attested Power of Attorney.

Prepare these documents immediately upon learning of a co-sharer's sale to an outsider:

  • Certified copy of the disputed Saf Kabala sale deed showing consideration price and registration date.
  • Warish (Succession) Certificate and ancestor's Khatian proving inheritance as a co-sharer in the holding.
  • Treasury Challan receipt confirming deposit of the full deed value plus statutory compensation (25% or 5%).
  • Updated Khajna (Land Development Tax) receipts and CS/SA/RS/BS Khatian records.
  • Proof of date of knowledge (e.g., Sub-Registry search slip or notice envelope) if no formal notice was served under Section 89.

For overseas heirs, our NRB Legal Help Desk coordinates rapid Sub-Registry checks and treasury deposits, or you can book a free initial consultation right away.

faqs.question: Can a co-sharer by purchase file a Section 96 pre-emption case in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Since the 2006 amendment to Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, only a co-sharer tenant by inheritance can claim pre-emption over agricultural land. Co-sharers by purchase and contiguous landowners are no longer eligible under Section 96.

faqs.question: What happens if the buyer refuses to disclose the sale to an NRB co-sharer?
faqs.answer: If no statutory notice was served on the co-sharer, the 2-month (SAT Act) or 4-month (NAT Act) limitation period runs from the date the co-sharer first gains actual knowledge of the sale, supported by credible documentary evidence.

faqs.question: Is pre-emption allowed if my brother gifted his share to his wife or son?
faqs.answer: Under Section 96(1) of the SAT Act, 1950, transfers by way of Heba (gift) to a spouse or blood relations within three degrees, as well as transfers by exchange, partition, or will, are exempt from pre-emption unless proved to be a disguised sale.

faqs.question: What if the buyer inflated the price in the sale deed to block pre-emption?
faqs.answer: If you suspect the deed consideration was artificially inflated to defeat your pre-emption right, you may plead the true market value and request the court under Section 96(4) to conduct an inquiry into the actual consideration paid.

faqs.question: Can a Muslim co-sharer claim Shufa if the 2-month SAT Act deadline is missed?
faqs.answer: In limited cases involving non-agricultural or urban property outside statutory bars, a claimant may invoke Muhammadan Law Shufa, provided they prove immediate performance of Talab-i-Mowasibat (immediate demand) and Talab-i-Ishhad (formal witness demand) within 1 year under Article 10, Limitation Act 1908.
